AUTHOR: Ditria
TITLE: Deep learning for automated analysis of fish abundance: the benefits of training across multiple habitats
REGION: Tweed River estuary, northern New South Wales, Australia
DATA: Own unbaited submerged action-camera footage from seagrass and rocky reef habitats (Feb 2019 - Mar 2020); ~4,700 training annotations per training set; two test sets of 48 videos (~1,500 annotations) each
V_EV: Discussion: 'While the seagrass datasets contain images with comparatively low background complexity, the water was often more turbid and picture clarity was thus affected'
D2: Three training sets (~4,700 annotations each: seagrass, reef, combination); two test sets of 48 videos each (~1,500 annotations)
D_EV: Methods, Datasets: 'The two test datasets in the different habitat types (seagrass and reef) were comprised of video footage that did not appear in the training data'
R_EV: Methods, Datasets: footage collected 'in the two most dissimilar habitats frequented by luderick, seagrass meadows and rocky reefs ... in the Tweed River estuary' (single estuary/campaign)
C_EV: no statement found (no confidence threshold, calibration or uncertainty reported; false positives only tabulated in Table 1)
E_EV: Methods, Performance measurements: 'Fish abundance performance was tested using MaxN ... Performance on MaxN was calculated by an F1 score'
METR: mAP50; MaxN F1 with TP/FP/FN counts per test set
NOTE: Full text coded is the bioRxiv preprint (May 2020) of the EMAS article; PEER coded from the published venue. R: cross-habitat test (seagrass <-> reef) with numeric drop (e.g. mAP50 91.7 -> 73.3) exists, but both habitats are in the same estuary and same campaign, so per P2 R1 = N; credited under D (video-level held-out). If a verifier counts habitat shift as external, R1 = Y, R2 = 사이트, R3 = Y, R_ALL = Y. C: no threshold reported; false positives tabulated and discussed briefly, so not N; coded NR. E4 = FNR because false negatives per test reported (Table 1). Ground truth is human annotation of the same videos.
